title: Lake Bosumtwi – the secrets of a crater lake

paragraphs.text: new project, led by Earth Sciences professor Christopher Scholz, is the first large-scale effort to study Lake Bosumtwi in Ghana, which was formed 1.1 million years ago when a giant meteor crashed into the Earth’s surface. The resulting crater is one of the largest and most well-preserved geologically young craters in the world, says Scholz, who is collaborating on the project with researchers from other universities. ‘Our data should provide information about what happens when an impact hits hard, pre-Cambrian rocks that are a billion years old,’ he says.

Equally important is the fact that the lake, which is about 8 kilometres in diameter, has no natural outlet. The rim of the crater rises about 250 metres above the water’s surface. Streams flow into the lake, Scholz says, but the water leaves only by evaporation, or by seeping through the lake sediment. For the past million years, the lake has acted as a tropical rain gauge, filling and drying with changes in precipitation and the tropical climate. The record of those changes is hidden in sediment below the lake bottom. ‘The lake is one of the best sites in the world for the study of tropical climate changes,’ Scholz says. ‘The tropics are the heat engine for the Earth’s climate. To understand global climate, we need to have records of climate changes from many sites around the world, including the tropics.’

Before the researchers could explore the lake’s subsurface, they needed a boat with a large working deck area that could carry eight tons of scientific equipment. The boat — named R/V Kalindi — was built in Florida in 1998. It was constructed in sizeable modules that were dismantled, packed inside a shipping container, and reassembled over a 10-day period in late November and early December 1999 in the rural village of Abono, Ghana. The research team then spent the next two weeks testing the boat and equipment before returning to the United States for the holidays.

In mid-January, five members of the team returned to Abono to begin collecting data about the lake’s subsurface using a technique called seismic reflection profiling. In this process, a high-pressure air gun is used to create small, pneumatic explosions in the water. The sound energy penetrates about 1,000 to 2,000 metres into the lake’s subsurface before bouncing back to the surface of the water. The reflected sound energy is detected by underwater microphones — called hydrophones — embedded in a long cable that is towed behind the boat as it crosses the lake in a grid pattern. One of the team’s main problems was navigating the fishing nets that criss-cross the lake’s surface. The sensitive equipment embedded in the cable would be damaged if it got tangled in the nets, so the team worked with local fishermen to clear the nets before the boat began its trajectory. On-board computers record the signals, and the resulting data are then processed in the laboratory. ‘The results will give us a good idea of the shape of the basin, how thick the layers of sediment are, and when and where there were major changes in sediment accumulation,’ Scholz says. ‘We are now developing a three-dimensional perspective of the lake’s subsurface.’

Team members spent about four weeks in Ghana collecting the data. Except for a few relatively minor adjustments, the equipment and the boat worked well. Problems that arose centred primarily around cultural barriers, and the consequential misunderstandings with local villagers.

Lake Bosumtwi, the largest natural freshwater lake in the country, is sacred to the Ashanti people, who believe their souls come to the lake to bid farewell to their god. Conventional canoes and boats are forbidden. Fishermen travel on the lake by floating on traditional planks they propel with small paddles. Before the research project could begin, Scholz and his Ghanaian counterparts had to secure special permission from tribal chiefs to put the R/V Kalindi on the lake.

Much of the data will be processed back in the laboratory using a technique called seismic reflection analysis. Scholz says, ‘The information we collect will be of tremendous benefit internationally to planetary geologists, palaeontologists, and other scientists from NASA.’

Preliminary analysis of the data, which was completed in May, uncovered the first substantiated example of the central uplift, Scholz says. According to scientists, smaller impacts are believed to create a simple bowl-shaped crater, while larger impacts may create a more complex shape featuring a central cone-like structure called the central uplift. Although scientists have been aware of their existence, concrete evidence of such structures had not previously been verified in craters on Earth. Scientists believe the meteor that formed Lake Bosumtwi was about 500 metres in diameter, or about the size of five football fields, and that the impact was intense enough to create the central uplift seen in the data analysis. As more of the data are analysed, additional details about the central uplift and the crater’s structure are expected to emerge, Scholz says.
